n:
*Study note:* *Psalm 31*. The psalmist confidently asks the Lord to protect him. Enemies threaten him and even his friends have abandoned him, but he looks to the Lord for vindication. In vv. 19-24, which were apparently written after the Lord answered the prayer of vv. 1-18, the psalmist thanks the Lord for delivering him.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “in your vindication rescue me.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “turn toward me your ear.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “become for me a rocky summit of refuge.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “a house of strongholds to deliver me.”

*Study note:* The metaphor of the *high ridge* pictures God as a rocky, relatively inaccessible summit, where one would be able to find protection from enemies. See {{1 Samuel 23:25|1 Sam 23:25}}, {{1 Samuel 23:28|28}}.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “name.” The Hebrew term שֵׁם (shem, “name”) refers here to the Lord’s reputation. (The English term “name” is often used the same way.)

*Translator's note:* The present translation assumes that the imperfect verbal forms are generalizing, “you lead me and guide me.” Other options are to take them as an expression of confidence about the future, “you will lead me and guide me” (cf. NASB), or as expressing a prayer, “lead me and guide me” (cf. NEB, NIV, NRSV).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “bring me out.” The translation assumes that the imperfect verbal form expresses the psalmist’s confidence about the future. Another option is to take the form as expressing a prayer, “free me.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “my spirit.” The noun רוּחַ (ruakh, “spirit”) here refers to the animating spirit that gives the psalmist life.

*Translator's note:* Or “redeem.” The perfect verbal form is understood here as anticipatory, indicating rhetorically the psalmist’s certitude and confidence that God will intervene. The psalmist is so confident of God’s positive response to his prayer that he can describe his deliverance as if it had already happened. Another option is to take the perfect as precative, expressing a wish or request (“rescue me”; cf. NIV). See *IBHS* 494-95 §30.5.4c, d. However, not all grammarians are convinced that the perfect is used as a precative in biblical Hebrew.
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “the ones who observe vain things of falsehood.” See {{Jonah 2:9|Jonah 2:9}}.
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “you know the distresses of my life.”
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “you cause my feet to stand.”

*Translator's note:* Or perhaps, “are swollen.”

*Translator's note:* Cf. {{Psalm 6:7|Ps 6:7}}, which has a similar line.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “my breath and my stomach [grow weak].” Apparently the verb in the previous line (“grow dim, be weakened”) is to be understood here. The Hebrew term נפשׁ can mean “life,” or, more specifically, “throat, breath.” The psalmist seems to be lamenting that his breathing is impaired because of the physical and emotional suffering he is forced to endure.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and my years in groaning.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “stumbles in.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “grow weak.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “because of all my enemies I am a reproach.”

*Text-critical note:* *Heb* “and to my neighbors, exceedingly.” If the MT is retained, then these words probably go with what precedes. However the syntactical awkwardness of the text suggests a revision may be needed. P. C. Craigie (*{{Psalm 1|Psalms 1-50}}* [WBC], 258) suggests that the initial mem (מ) on מְאֹד (meʾod, “exceedingly”) be understood as an enclitic mem (ם) which was originally suffixed to the preceding form and then later misinterpreted. The resulting form אֵד (ʾed) can then be taken as a defectively written form of אֵיד (ʾed, “calamity”). If one follows this emendation, then the text reads literally, “and to my neighbors [I am one who experiences] calamity.” The noun פַחַד (fakhad, “[object of] horror”) occurs in the next line; אֵיד and פַחַד appear in parallelism elsewhere (see {{Proverbs 1:26|Prov 1:26-27}}).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and [an object of ] horror to those known by me.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “I am forgotten, like a dead man, from [the] heart.” The “heart” is here viewed as the center of one’s thoughts.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “I am like a broken jar.” One throws away a broken jar without a second thought because it is considered worthless and useless.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “the report of many.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “the terror from all around.”

*Translator's note:* The verb יִדְּמוּ (yiddemu) is understood as a form of דָּמַם (damam, “wail, lament”). Another option is to take the verb from דָּמַם (“be quiet”; see BDB 198-99 s.v. I דָּמַם), in which case one might translate, “May they lie silent in the grave.”

*Translator's note:* Or “How abundant are your blessings!”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “for those who fear you.”

*Translator's note:* “Taking shelter” in the Lord is an idiom for seeking his protection. Seeking his protection presupposes and even demonstrates the subject’s loyalty to the Lord. In the psalms those who “take shelter” in the Lord are contrasted with the wicked and equated with those who love, fear, and serve the Lord ({{Psalm 2:12|Pss 2:12}}; {{Psalm 5:11|5:11-12}}; {{Psalm 34:21|34:21-22}}).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “you work [your favor] for the ones seeking shelter in you before the sons of men.”

*Translator's note:* The noun רֹכֶס (rokhes) occurs only here. Its meaning is debated; some suggest “snare,” while others propose “slander” or “conspiracy.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “you hide them in the hiding place of your face from the attacks of man.” The imperfect verbal forms in this verse draw attention to God’s typical treatment of the faithful.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “you conceal them in a shelter from the strife of tongues.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “blessed [be] the Lord.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “for he caused his faithfulness to be amazing to me in a besieged city.” The psalmist probably speaks figuratively here. He compares his crisis to being trapped in a besieged city, but the Lord answered his prayer for help. Verses {{Psalm 31:19|19-24}} were apparently written after the Lord answered the prayer of vv. {{Psalm 31:1|1-18}}.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and I, I said in my haste.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “from before your eyes.”

*Translator's note:* A “faithful follower” (חָסִיד, khasid) is one who does what is right in God’s eyes and remains faithful to God (see {{Psalm 4:3|Pss 4:3}}; {{Psalm 12:1|12:1}}; {{Psalm 16:10|16:10}}; {{Psalm 31:23|31:23}}; {{Psalm 37:28|37:28}}; {{Psalm 86:2|86:2}}; {{Psalm 97:10|97:10}}).

*Translator's note:* The participial forms in the second and third lines characterize the Lord as one who typically protects the faithful and judges the proud.
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “be strong and let your heart[s] be confident.”

*Study note:* *Psalm 32*. The psalmist recalls the agony he experienced prior to confessing his sins and affirms that true happiness comes when one’s sins are forgiven. He then urges others not to be stubborn, but to turn to God while forgiveness is available, for God extends his mercy to the repentant, while the wicked experience nothing but sorrow.

*Translator's note:* The meaning of the Hebrew term מַשְׂכִּיל (maskil) is uncertain. The word is derived from a verb meaning “to be prudent; to be wise.” Various options are: “a contemplative song,” “a song imparting moral wisdom,” or “a skillful [i.e., well-written] song.” The term occurs in the superscriptions of {{Psalm 32|Pss 32}}, {{Psalm 42|42}}, {{Psalm 44|44}}, {{Psalm 45|45}}, {{Psalm 52|52-55}}, {{Psalm 74|74}}, {{Psalm 78|78}}, {{Psalm 88|88}}, {{Psalm 89|89}}, and {{Psalm 142|142}}, as well as in {{Psalm 47:7|Ps 47:7}}.

*Translator's note:* The Hebrew noun is an abstract plural. The word often refers metonymically to the happiness that God-given security and prosperity produce (see {{Psalm 1:1|Pss 1:1}}, {{Psalm 1:3|3}}; {{Psalm 2:12|2:12}}; {{Psalm 34:9|34:9}}; {{Psalm 41:1|41:1}}; {{Psalm 65:4|65:4}}; {{Psalm 84:12|84:12}}; {{Psalm 89:15|89:15}}; {{Psalm 106:3|106:3}}; {{Psalm 112:1|112:1}}; {{Psalm 127:5|127:5}}; {{Psalm 128:1|128:1}}; {{Psalm 144:15|144:15}}). Here it refers to the relief that one experiences when one’s sins are forgiven.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “lifted up.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “covered over.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “man.” The word choice reflects the perspective of the psalmist, who is male. The principle of the psalm is certainly applicable to all people, regardless of their gender or age. To facilitate modern application, the gender and age specific “man” has been translated with the more neutral “one.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “blessed [is] the man to whom the Lord does not impute wrongdoing.”

*Study note:* *In whose spirit there is no deceit*. The point is not that the individual is sinless and pure. In this context, which focuses on confession and forgiveness of sin, the psalmist refers to one who refuses to deny or hide his sin, but instead honestly confesses it to God.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “when I was silent.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “my bones became brittle.” The psalmist pictures himself as aging and growing physically weak. Trying to cover up his sin brought severe physical consequences.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “your hand was heavy upon me.”

*Study note:* *You tried to destroy me*. The psalmist’s statement reflects his perspective. As far as he was concerned, it seemed as if the Lord was trying to kill him.

*Text-critical note:* *Heb* “my [?] was turned.” The meaning of the Hebrew term לְשַׁד (leshad) is uncertain. A noun לָשָׁד (lashad, “cake”) is attested in {{Numbers 11:8|Num 11:8}}, but it would make no sense to understand that word in this context. It is better to emend the form to לְשֻׁדִּי (leshuddi, “to my destruction”) and understand “your hand” as the subject of the verb “was turned.” In this case the text reads, “[your hand] was turned to my destruction.” In Lam 3:3 the author laments that God’s “hand” was “turned” (הָפַךְ, hafakh) against him in a hostile sense.

*Translator's note:* The translation assumes that the plural form indicates degree. If one understands the form as a true plural, then one might translate, “in the times of drought.”

*Study note:* *Summer*. Perhaps the psalmist suffered during the hot season and perceived the very weather as being an instrument of divine judgment. Another option is that he compares his time of suffering to the uncomfortable and oppressive heat of summer.

*Translator's note:* The Hiphil of ידה normally means “give thanks, praise,” but here, as in {{Proverbs 28:13|Prov 28:13}}, it means “confess.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “the wrongdoing of my sin.” By joining synonyms for “sin” in this way, the psalmist may be emphasizing the degree of his wrongdoing.

*Translator's note:* A “faithful follower” (חָסִיד, khasid) is one who does what is right in God’s eyes and remains faithful to God (see {{Psalm 4:3|Pss 4:3}}; {{Psalm 12:1|12:1}}; {{Psalm 18:25|18:25}}; {{Psalm 31:23|31:23}}; {{Psalm 37:28|37:28}}; {{Psalm 86:2|86:2}}; {{Psalm 97:10|97:10}}).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “at a time of finding.” This may mean, “while there is time to ‘find’ [the Lord]” and seek his forgiveness (cf. NIV). Some emend the text by combining מְצֹא (metsoʾ, “finding”) with the following term רַק (raq, “only, surely”) and read either ר[וֹ]מָצ (matsor, “distress”; see {{Psalm 31:22|Ps 31:22}}) or ק[וֹ]מָצ (matsoq, “hardship”; see {{Psalm 119:143|Ps 119:143}}). In this case, one may translate “in a time of distress/hardship” (cf. NEB, NRSV).

*Translator's note:* The Hebrew term רַק (raq) occasionally has an asseverative force.

*Study note:* The *surging water* is here a metaphor for trouble that endangers one’s life.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “him.” The translation uses the plural “them” to agree with the plural “every one of your faithful followers” in the first line of v. {{Psalm 32:6|6}}.
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “[with] shouts of joy of deliverance you surround me.”

*Translator's note:* The second person pronominal forms in this verse are singular. The psalmist addresses each member of his audience individually (see also the note on the word “eye” in the next line). A less likely option (but one which is commonly understood) is that the Lord addresses the psalmist in vv. {{Psalm 32:8|8-9}} (cf. NASB “I will instruct you and teach you…I will counsel you with My eye upon you”).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “I will instruct you and I will teach you in the way [in] which you should walk.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “I will advise, upon you my eye,” that is, “I will offer advice [with] my eye upon you.” In 2 Chr 20:12 the statement “our eye is upon you” means that the speakers are looking to the Lord for intervention. Here the expression “my eye upon you” may simply mean that the psalmist will teach his pupils directly and personally.

*Translator's note:* The verb form is plural (i.e., “do not all of you be”); the psalmist addresses the whole group.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “like a horse, like a mule without understanding.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “with a bridle and bit, its [?] to hold, not to come near to you.” The meaning of the Hebrew noun עֲדִי (ʿadiy) is uncertain. Normally the word refers to “jewelry,” so some suggest the meaning “trappings” here (cf. NASB). Some emend the form to לְחֵיהֶם (lekhehem, “their jawbones”) but it is difficult to see how the present Hebrew text, even if defective, could have derived from this proposed original reading. P. C. Craigie (*{{Psalm 1|Psalms 1-50}}* [WBC], 265) takes the form from an Arabic root and translates “whose gallop.” Cf. also NRSV “whose temper must be curbed.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “many [are the] pains of evil [one].” The singular form is representative here; the typical evildoer, representative of the larger group of wicked people, is in view.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “but the one who trusts in the Lord, faithfulness surrounds him.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “all [you] pure of heart.” The “heart” is here viewed as the seat of one’s moral character and motives. The “pure of heart” are God’s faithful followers who trust in and love the Lord and, as a result, experience his deliverance (see {{Psalm 7:10|Pss 7:10}}; {{Psalm 11:2|11:2}}; {{Psalm 36:10|36:10}}; {{Psalm 64:10|64:10}}; {{Psalm 94:15|94:15}}; {{Psalm 97:11|97:11}}).
*Study note:* *Psalm 33*. In this hymn the psalmist praises the Lord as the sovereign creator and just ruler of the world who protects and vindicates those who fear him.

*Study note:* A *new song* is appropriate because the Lord is constantly intervening in the lives of his people in fresh and exciting ways.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “play skillfully with a loud shout.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “word.” In this context, which depicts the Lord as the sovereign creator and ruler of the world, the Lord’s “word” refers to the decrees whereby he governs his dominion.

*Translator's note:* Or “upright.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and all his work [is done] with faithfulness.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “loves.” The verb “loves” is here metonymic; the Lord’s commitment to principles of equity and justice causes him to actively promote these principles as he governs the world.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “fills the earth.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “word.”

*Translator's note:* The word רוּחַ (ruakh, “spirit, wind, breath”) is used in the creation account in {{Genesis 1:2|Gen 1:2}} “the Spirit of God was moving.” Here parallel to “decree/word,” it recalls the account of God speaking in order to create (cf. {{Genesis 1:14|Gen 1:14}}).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “[he] gathers like a pile the waters of the sea.” Some prefer to emend נֵד (ned, “heap, pile”; cf. NASB) to נֹד (nod, “bottle”; cf. NRSV; NIV “into jars”), but “pile” is used elsewhere to describe water that the Lord confines to one place ({{Exodus 15:8|Exod 15:8}}; {{Joshua 3:13|Josh 3:13}}, {{Joshua 3:16|16}}; {{Psalm 78:13|Ps 78:13}}). This verse appears to refer to {{Genesis 1:9|Gen 1:9}}, where God decrees that the watery deep be gathered to one place so that dry land might appear. If so, the participles in this and the following line depict this action with special vividness, as if the reader were present on the occasion. Another option is that the participles picture the confinement of the sea to one place as an ongoing divine activity.

*Translator's note:* Or “watery depths.” The form תְּהוֹמוֹת (tehomot, “watery depths”) is the plural form of תְּהוֹם (tehom, “great deep”; see {{Genesis 1:2|Gen 1:2}}).
*Translator's note:* In this context “fear” probably means “to demonstrate respect for the Lord’s power and authority by worshiping him and obeying his commandments.”

*Translator's note:* That is, “all the earth” in the first line of v. {{Psalm 33:8|8}}. The apparent antecedent of the masculine subject of the verbs in v. {{Psalm 33:9|9}} (note וַיֶּהִי [vayyehiy] and וַיַּעֲמֹד [vayyaʿamod]) is “earth” or “world,” both of which are feminine nouns. However, כָּל (kol, “all”) may be the antecedent, or the apparent lack of agreement may be explained by the collective nature of the nouns involved here (see GKC 463 §145.*e*).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “he commanded.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “breaks” or “destroys.” The Hebrew perfect verbal forms here and in the next line generalize about the Lord’s activity.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “thoughts.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “the thoughts of his heart for generation to generation.” The verb “abides” is supplied in the translation. The Lord’s “decisions” and “plans” here refer to his decrees and purposes.

*Translator's note:* The Hebrew noun is an abstract plural. The word often refers metonymically to the happiness that God-given security and prosperity produce (see {{Psalm 1:1|Pss 1:1}}; {{Psalm 2:12|2:12}}; {{Psalm 34:9|34:9}}; {{Psalm 41:1|41:1}}; {{Psalm 65:4|65:4}}; {{Psalm 84:12|84:12}}; {{Psalm 89:15|89:15}}; {{Psalm 106:3|106:3}}; {{Psalm 112:1|112:1}}; {{Psalm 127:5|127:5}}; {{Psalm 128:1|128:1}}; {{Psalm 144:15|144:15}}).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “inheritance.”

*Translator's note:* The Hebrew perfect verbal forms in v. {{Psalm 33:13|13}} state general facts.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “all the sons of men.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “the one who forms together their heart[s].” “Heart” here refers to human nature, composed of intellect, emotions and will. The precise force of יָחַד (yakhad, “together”) is unclear here. The point seems to be that the Lord is the creator of every human being.
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “a lie [is] the horse for victory.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “look, the eye of the Lord [is] toward the ones who fear him.” The expression “the eye…[is] toward” here indicates recognition and the bestowing of favor. See {{Psalm 34:15|Ps 34:15}}. The one who fears the Lord respects his sovereignty and obeys his commandments. See {{Psalm 128:1|Ps 128:1}}; {{Proverbs 14:2|Prov 14:2}}.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “for the ones who wait for his faithfulness.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “to save from death their live[s].”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and to keep them alive in famine.”

*Translator's note:* Or “our lives.” The suffixed form of נֶפֶשׁ (nefesh, “being, life”) is often equivalent to a pronoun in poetic texts.

*Translator's note:* Or “[source of] help.”

*Translator's note:* Or “protector.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “let your faithfulness, O Lord, be on us.”

*Translator's note:* Or “just as.”

*Study note:* In this song of thanksgiving the psalmist praises God for delivering him from distress. He encourages others to be loyal to the Lord, tells them how to please God, and assures them that the Lord protects his servants. The psalm is an acrostic; vv. 1-21 begin with successive letters of the Hebrew alphabet. (Verse 6 begins with the letter he (ה) and v. 7 with the letter zayin (ז). The letter vav (ו), which comes between ה and ז, seems to be omitted, although it does appear at the beginning of v. 6b. The final verse of the psalm, which begins with the letter pe (פ), is outside the acrostic scheme.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “By David, when he changed his sense before Abimelech and he drove him away and he went.”

*Study note:* *Pretended to be insane*. The psalm heading appears to refer to the account in {{1 Samuel 21:10|1 Sam 21:10-15}} which tells how David, fearful that King Achish of Gath might kill him, pretended to be insane in hopes that the king would simply send him away. The psalm heading names the king Abimelech, not Achish, suggesting that the tradition is confused on this point. However, perhaps “Abimelech” was a royal title, rather than a proper name. See P. C. Craigie, *{{Psalm 1|Psalms 1-50}}* (WBC), 278.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “bless.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “continually [will] his praise [be] in my mouth.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “my soul will boast”; or better, “let my soul boast.” Following the cohortative form in v. {{Psalm 34:1|1}}, it is likely that the prefixed verbal form here is jussive.

*Translator's note:* The two prefixed verbal forms in this verse are best taken as jussives, for the psalmist is calling his audience to worship (see v. {{Psalm 34:3|3}}).

*Text-critical note:* The translation follows the LXX. The MT reads “they looked to him and were radiant; let their faces not be ashamed.” The MT reads the first verb as a perfect (הִבִּיטוּ, hibbitu), which would be past time, while the LXX (supported by Aquila, the Syriac, Jerome, and some medieval Hebrew mss) reads an imperative (הַבִּיטוּ, habbitu). The MT reads the second verb as a vav plus perfect, while the LXX reads it as an imperative, again a difference of the initial vowel. The third verb is a jussive preceded by אַל (ʾal), which supports reading the first two as imperatives. The second masculine plural pronoun (“your faces”) of the LXX and the Syriac, matches this understanding of the preceding verbs. The MT reading (“their faces”) is consistent with its view of the previous verbs. The reading adopted here interprets the verse as interrupting a testimony given to the congregation with an admonition based on that testimony.
*Translator's note:* The pronoun refers back to “this oppressed man,” namely, the psalmist.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “his”; the referent (the Lord) has been specified in the translation for clarity.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “those who fear him.”

*Translator's note:* The prefixed verb with vav (ו) consecutive here carries the same generalizing force as the active participle in the first line. See GKC 329 §111.*u*.

*Translator's note:* This verb is normally used of tasting food, as in eating a little bit of food ({{1 Samuel 14:43|1 Sam 14:43}}; {{Jonah 3:7|Jonah 3:7}}) or evaluating it ({{Job 12:11|Job 12:11}}; {{Job 34:3|34:3}}). The two references to the physical senses stand for invitation and realization. Even a small or beginning experience of God reveals that he is good.

*Translator's note:* The Hebrew noun is an abstract plural. The word often refers metonymically to the happiness that God-given security and prosperity produce (see {{Psalm 1:1|Pss 1:1}}, {{Psalm 1:3|3}}; {{Psalm 2:12|2:12}}; {{Psalm 41:1|41:1}}; {{Psalm 65:4|65:4}}; {{Psalm 84:12|84:12}}; {{Psalm 89:15|89:15}}; {{Psalm 106:3|106:3}}; {{Psalm 112:1|112:1}}; {{Psalm 127:5|127:5}}; {{Psalm 128:1|128:1}}; {{Psalm 144:15|144:15}}).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “man.” The principle of the psalm is certainly applicable to all people, regardless of their gender or age. To facilitate modern application, we translate the gender and age specific “man” with the more neutral “one.”

*Translator's note:* “Taking shelter” in the Lord is an idiom for seeking his protection. Seeking his protection presupposes and even demonstrates the subject’s loyalty to the Lord. In the psalms those who “take shelter” in the Lord are contrasted with the wicked and equated with those who love, fear, and serve the Lord ({{Psalm 2:12|Pss 2:12}}; {{Psalm 5:11|5:11-12}}; {{Psalm 31:17|31:17-20}}; {{Psalm 34:21|34:21-22}}).
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “the fear of the Lord I will teach you.” In vv. {{Psalm 34:13|13-14}} the psalmist explains to his audience what it means to “fear” the Lord.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “Who is the man who desires life?” The rhetorical question is used to grab the audience’s attention. “Life” probably refers here to quality of life, not just physical existence or even duration of life. See the following line.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “[Who] loves days to see good?”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “guard your tongue from evil.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and your lips from speaking deception.”

*Translator's note:* Or “do good.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “seek peace and pursue it.”
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “the eyes of the Lord [are] toward the godly, and his ears [are] toward their cry for help.”
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “the face of the Lord [is] against the doers of evil to cut off from the earth memory of them.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “they” (i.e., the godly mentioned in v. {{Psalm 34:15|15}}).

*Translator's note:* The three perfect verbal forms are taken in a generalizing sense in v. {{Psalm 34:17|17}} and translated with the present tense (note the generalizing mood of vv. {{Psalm 34:18|18-22}}).

*Translator's note:* The Hebrew imperfect verbal form highlights the generalizing statement and draws attention to the fact that the Lord typically delivers the oppressed and needy.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “the crushed in spirit.”

*Translator's note:* The Hebrew text uses the singular form; the representative or typical godly person is envisioned.

*Translator's note:* Or “trials.”

*Translator's note:* The Hebrew imperfect verbal form highlights the generalizing statement and draws attention to the fact that the Lord typically delivers the godly.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “him,” agreeing with the singular form in the preceding line.

*Study note:* *Not one of them is broken*. The author of the Gospel of John saw a fulfillment of these words in Jesus’ experience on the cross (see {{John 19:31|John 19:31-37}}), for the Roman soldiers, when they saw that Jesus was already dead, did not break his legs as was customarily done to speed the death of crucified individuals. John’s use of the psalm seems strange, for the statement in its original context suggests that the Lord protects the godly from physical harm. Jesus’ legs may have remained unbroken, but he was brutally and unjustly executed by his enemies. John seems to give the statement a literal sense that is foreign to its original literary context by applying a promise of divine protection to a man who was seemingly not saved by God. However, John saw in this incident a foreshadowing of Jesus’ ultimate deliverance and vindication. His unbroken bones were a reminder of God’s commitment to the godly and a sign of things to come. Jesus’ death on the cross was not the end of the story; God vindicated him, as John goes on to explain in the following context ({{John 19:38|John 19:38-20:18}}).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “the Lord does not abandon him into his hand or condemn him when he is judged.” The imperfects draw attention to the Lord’s characteristic behavior in this regard.

*Translator's note:* Or “wait.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “keep his way.” The Lord’s “way” refers here to the “conduct required” by the Lord. In {{Psalm 25|Ps 25}} the Lord’s “ways” are associated with his covenantal demands (see vv. {{Psalm 37:4|4}}, {{Psalm 37:9|9-10}}). See also {{Psalm 119:3|Ps 119:3}} (cf. vv. {{Psalm 37:1|1}}, {{Psalm 37:4|4}}), as well as {{Deuteronomy 8:6|Deut 8:6}}; {{Deuteronomy 10:12|10:12}}; {{Deuteronomy 11:22|11:22}}; {{Deuteronomy 19:9|19:9}}; {{Deuteronomy 26:17|26:17}}; {{Deuteronomy 28:9|28:9}}; {{Deuteronomy 30:16|30:16}}.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and he will lift you up.” The prefixed verbal form with *vav* (ו) is best taken here as a result clause following the imperatives in the preceding lines.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “when evil men are cut off you will see.”

*Translator's note:* The Hebrew uses the representative singular again here.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “being exposed [?] like a native, luxuriant.” The Hebrew form מִתְעָרֶה (mitʿareh) appears to be a Hitpael participle from עָרָה (ʿarah, “be exposed”), but this makes no sense in this context. Perhaps the form is a dialectal variant of מִתְעָלָה (“giving oneself an air of importance”; see Jer 51:3), from עָלָה (ʿalah, “go up”; see P. C. Craigie, *{{Psalm 1|Psalms 1-50}}* [WBC], 296). The noun אֶזְרָח (ʾezrakh, “native, full citizen”) refers elsewhere to people, but here, where it is collocated with “luxuriant, green,” it probably refers to a tree growing in native soil.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and he passes by and, look, he is not [there].” The subject of the verb “passes by” is probably indefinite, referring to any passerby. Some prefer to change the form to first person, “and I passed by” (cf. NEB; note the first person verbal forms in preceding verse and in the following line).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “for [there is] an end for a man of peace.” Some interpret אַחֲרִית (ʾakharit, “end”) as referring to offspring (see the next verse and {{Psalm 109:13|Ps 109:13}}; cf. NEB, NRSV).

*Translator's note:* Or “destroyed together.” In this case the psalmist pictures judgment sweeping them away as a group.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “the end of evil men is cut off.” As in v. {{Psalm 37:37|37}}, some interpret אַחֲרִית (ʾakharit, “end”) as referring to offspring (see {{Psalm 109:13|Ps 109:13}}). The perfect verbal forms in v. {{Psalm 37:38|38}} probably express general truths. Another option is that they are used emphatically to state with certitude that the demise of the wicked is as good as done.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and the deliverance of the godly [ones] [is] from the Lord.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “[he is] their place of refuge in a time of trouble.”
*Translator's note:* The prefixed verbal forms with vav (ו) consecutive carry on the generalizing tone of the preceding verse.

*Study note:* *Psalm 38*. The author asks the Lord to deliver him from his enemies. He confesses his sin and recognizes that the crisis he faces is the result of divine discipline. Yet he begs the Lord not to reject him.

*Translator's note:* The Hebrew text reads simply, “to cause to remember.” The same form, the Hiphil infinitive of זָכַר (zakhar, “remember”), also appears in the heading of {{Psalm 70|Ps 70}}. Some understand this in the sense of “for the memorial offering,” but it may carry the idea of bringing one’s plight to God’s attention (see P. C. Craigie, *{{Psalm 1|Psalms 1-50}}* [WBC], 303).

*Study note:* Cf. {{Psalm 38:1|Ps 38:1}} with {{Psalm 6:1|Ps 6:1}}, which has similar wording.

*Translator's note:* The words “continue to” are supplied in the translation of both lines. The following verses make it clear that the psalmist is already experiencing divine rebuke/punishment. He asks that it might cease.

*Translator's note:* The verb Hebrew נָחַת (nakhat) apparently here means “penetrate, pierce” (note the use of the Qal in {{Proverbs 17:10|Prov 17:10}}). The psalmist pictures the Lord as a warrior who shoots arrows at him (see {{Psalm 7:12|Ps 7:12-13}}).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and your hand [?] upon me.” The meaning of the verb נָחַת (nakhat) is unclear in this context. It could mean “your hand comes down on me.” It may be preferable to emend the form to וַתָּנַח (vattanakh) from the verb נוּחַ (nuakh, “rest”). In this case the text would read literally, “and your hand rests upon me” (see {{Isaiah 25:10|Isa 25:10}}, though the phrase is used in a positive sense there, unlike {{Psalm 38:2|Ps 38:2}}).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “there is no soundness in my flesh from before your anger.” “Anger” here refers metonymically to divine judgment, which is the practical effect of God’s anger at the psalmist’s sin.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “there is no health in my bones from before my sin.”

*Study note:* The reference to *wounds* may be an extension of the metaphorical language of v. {{Psalm 38:2|2}}. The psalmist pictures himself as one whose flesh is ripped and torn by arrows.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “my wounds stink, they are festering” (cf. NEB).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “from before my foolishness.”

*Translator's note:* The verb’s precise shade of meaning in this context is not entirely clear. The verb, which literally means “to bend,” may refer to the psalmist’s posture. In {{Isaiah 21:3|Isa 21:3}} it seems to mean “be confused, dazed.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “I am bowed down to excess.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “for my loins are filled with shame.” The “loins” are viewed here as the seat of the psalmist’s emotions. The present translation assumes that נִקְלֶה (niqleh) is derived from קָלָה (qalah, “be dishonored”). Some derive it instead from a homonymic root קָלָה (qalah), meaning “to roast.” In this case one might translate “fever” (cf. NEB “my loins burn with fever”).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “there is no soundness in my flesh” (see v. {{Psalm 38:3|3}}).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “I am numb and crushed to excess.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “I roar because of the moaning of my heart.”
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “O Lord, before you [is] all my desire.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and the light of my eyes, even they, there is not with me.” The “light of the eyes” may refer to physical energy (see {{1 Samuel 14:27|1 Sam 14:27}}, {{1 Samuel 14:29|29}}), life itself ({{Psalm 13:3|Ps 13:3}}), or the ability to see ({{Proverbs 29:23|Prov 29:23}}).

*Translator's note:* Or “wound,” or “illness.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “stand [aloof].”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and the ones near me off at a distance stand.”
*Study note:* *I am like a deaf man…like a mute*. The psalmist is like a deaf mute; he is incapable of defending himself and is vulnerable to his enemies’ deception (see v. {{Psalm 38:14|14}}).
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and there is not in his mouth arguments.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “For I said, ‘Lest they rejoice over me.’” The psalmist recalls the motivating argument of his petition. He probably prefaced this statement with a prayer for deliverance (see {{Psalm 7:1|Pss 7:1-2}}; {{Psalm 13:3|13:3-4}}; {{Psalm 28:1|28:1}}).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “they will magnify against me.” See {{Psalm 35:26|Pss 35:26}}; {{Psalm 55:13|55:13}}.
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and my pain [is] before me continually.”
*Translator's note:* Or “for.” The translation assumes that כִּי (ki) is asseverative here.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and my enemies, life, are many.” The noun חַיִּים (khayyim, “life”) fits very awkwardly here. The translation assumes an emendation to חִנָּם (khinnam, “without reason”; note the parallelism with שֶׁקֶר [sheqer, “falsely”] and see {{Psalm 35:19|Pss 35:19}}; {{Psalm 69:4|69:4}}; Lam 3:52). The verb עָצַם (ʿatsam) can sometimes mean “are strong,” but here it probably focuses on numerical superiority (note the parallel verb רָבַב, ravav, “be many”).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “are many.”
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “the ones who repay evil instead of good accuse me, instead of my pursuing good.”

*Study note:* *Psalm 39*. The psalmist laments his frailty and mortality as he begs the Lord to take pity on him and remove his disciplinary hand.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “I said.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “I will watch my ways, from sinning with my tongue.”

*Study note:* The psalmist wanted to voice a lament to the Lord (see vv. {{Psalm 38:4|4-6}}), but he hesitated to do so in the presence of evil people, for such words might be sinful if they gave the wicked an occasion to insult God. See C. A. Briggs and E. G. Briggs, *Psalms* (ICC), 1:345.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “I was mute [with] silence.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “I was quiet from good.” He kept quiet, resisting the urge to find emotional release and satisfaction by voicing his lament.

*Study note:* *I held back the urge to speak*. For a helpful discussion of the relationship (and tension) between silence and complaint in ancient Israelite lamentation, see E. S. Gerstenberger, *Psalms, Part I* (FOTL), 166-67.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and my pain was stirred up.” Emotional pain is in view here.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “my heart was hot within me.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “In my reflection fire burned.” The prefixed verbal form is either a preterite (past tense) or an imperfect being used in a past progressive or customary sense (“fire was burning”).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “I spoke with my tongue.” The phrase “these words” is supplied in the translation for clarification and for stylistic reasons.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “Cause me to know, O Lord, my end; and the measure of my days, what it is!”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “Let me know how transient I am.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “Look, handbreadths you make my days.” The “handbreadth” (equivalent to the width of four fingers) was one of the smallest measures used by ancient Israelites. See P. C. Craigie, *{{Psalm 1|Psalms 1-50}}* (WBC), 309.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “is like nothing before you.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “surely, all vapor [is] all mankind, standing firm.” Another option is to translate, “Surely, all mankind, though seemingly secure, is nothing but a vapor.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “surely, as an image man walks about.” The preposition prefixed to “image” indicates identity here.

*Study note:* *People go through life* (*Heb* “man walks about”). “Walking” is here used as a metaphor for living. The point is that human beings are here today, gone tomorrow. They have no lasting substance and are comparable to mere images or *ghosts*.

*Text-critical note:* *Heb* “Surely [in] vain they strive, he accumulates and does not know who gathers them.” The MT as it stands is syntactically awkward. The verb forms switch from singular (“walks about”) to plural (“they strive”) and then back to singular (“accumulates and does not know”), even though the subject (generic “man”) remains the same. Furthermore there is no object for the verb “accumulates” and no plural antecedent for the plural pronoun (“them”) attached to “gathers.” These problems can be removed if one emends the text from הֶבֶל יֶהֱמָיוּן (hevel yehemayun, “[in] vain they strive”) to הֶבְלֵי הָמוֹן (hevle hamon, “vain things of wealth”). The present translation follows this emendation.
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “because you acted.” The psalmist has in mind God’s disciplinary measures (see vv. {{Psalm 38:10|10-13}}).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “remove from upon me your wound.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “from the hostility of your hand I have come to an end.”

*Translator's note:* “with punishments on account of sin you discipline a man.”

*Text-critical note:* *Heb* “you cause to dissolve, like a moth, his desired [thing].” The translation assumes an emendation of חֲמוּדוֹ (khamudo, “his desirable [thing]”) to חֶמְדוֹ (khemdo, “his loveliness” [or “beauty”]), a reading that is supported by a few medieval Hebrew mss.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “do not be deaf to my tears.”

*Translator's note:* The Hebrew terms גֵּר (ger, “resident foreigner”) and תּוֹשָׁב (toshav, “resident/dweller”) have similar meanings. They are not used here with the technical distinctions of most references in Mosaic Law. {{Psalm 39:12|Ps 39:12}} takes up this language from Lev 25:23 where the terms emphasize that Israel would be a guest on God’s land. They were attached to the Lord’s household; they did not own the land. The Psalmist identifies himself with this privileged yet dependent position. Abraham also refers to himself by these terms in {{Genesis 23:4|Gen 23:4}}.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “Gaze away from me and I will smile before I go and am not.” The precise identification of the initial verb form (הָשַׁע, hashaʿ) is uncertain. It could be from the root שָׁעָע (shaʿaʿ, “smear over”), but “your eyes” would be the expected object in this case (see {{Isaiah 6:10|Isa 6:10}}). The verb may be an otherwise unattested Hiphil form of שָׁעָה (shaʿah, “to gaze”) meaning “cause your gaze to be.” Some prefer to emend the form to the Qal שְׁעֵה (sheʿeh, “gaze”; see {{Job 14:6|Job 14:6}}). If one does read a form of the verb “to gaze,” the angry divine “gaze” of discipline would seem to be in view (see vv. {{Psalm 39:10|10-11}}). For a similar expression of this sentiment see {{Job 10:20|Job 10:20-21}}.

*Study note:* *Psalm 40*. The psalmist combines a song of thanksgiving for a recent act of divine deliverance (vv. 1-11) with a confident petition for renewed divine intervention (vv. 12-17).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “relying, I relied.” The infinitive absolute precedes the finite verbal form to emphasize the verbal idea. The emphasis is reflected in the translation through the adverb “completely.” Another option is to translate, “I waited patiently” (cf. NASB, NIV, NRSV).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “cistern of roaring.” The Hebrew noun בּוֹר (bor, “cistern, pit”) is used metaphorically here of Sheol, the place of death, which is sometimes depicted as a raging sea (see {{Psalm 18:4|Ps 18:4}}, {{Psalm 18:15|15-16}}). The noun שָׁאוֹן (shaʾon, “roaring”) refers elsewhere to the crashing sound of the sea’s waves (see {{Psalm 65:7|Ps 65:7}}).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “from the mud of mud.” The Hebrew phrase translated “slimy mud” employs an appositional genitive. Two synonyms are joined in a construct relationship to emphasize the single idea. For a detailed discussion of the grammatical point with numerous examples, see Y. Avishur, “Pairs of Synonymous Words in the Construct State (and in Appositional Hendiadys) in Biblical Hebrew,” *Semitics* 2 (1971): 17-81.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “he established my footsteps.”

*Study note:* A *new song* was appropriate because the Lord had intervened in the psalmist’s experience in a fresh and exciting way.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and he placed in my mouth a new song, praise to our God.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “may many see and fear and trust in the Lord.” The translation assumes that the initial prefixed verbal form is a jussive (“may many see”), rather than an imperfect (“many will see”). The following prefixed verbal forms with vav (ו) conjunctive are taken as indicating purpose or result (“so that they might swear allegiance…and trust”) after the introductory jussive.

*Translator's note:* The Hebrew noun is an abstract plural. The word often refers metonymically to the happiness that God-given security and prosperity produce (see {{Psalm 1:1|Pss 1:1}}, {{Psalm 1:3|3}}; {{Psalm 2:12|2:12}}; {{Psalm 34:9|34:9}}; {{Psalm 41:1|41:1}}; {{Psalm 65:4|65:4}}; {{Psalm 84:12|84:12}}; {{Psalm 89:15|89:15}}; {{Psalm 106:3|106:3}}; {{Psalm 112:1|112:1}}; {{Psalm 127:5|127:5}}; {{Psalm 128:1|128:1}}; {{Psalm 144:15|144:15}}).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “man.” See the note on the word “one” in {{Psalm 1:1|Ps 1:1}}.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “who has made the Lord his [object of] trust.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and does not turn toward.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “those falling away toward a lie.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “many things you have done, you, O Lord my God, your amazing deeds and your thoughts toward us.” The precise meaning of the text is not clear, but the psalmist seems to be recalling the Lord’s miraculous deeds on Israel’s behalf (see {{Psalm 9:1|Pss 9:1}}; {{Psalm 26:7|26:7}}), as well as his covenantal decrees and promises (see {{Psalm 33:11|Ps 33:11}}).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “there is none arrayed against you.” The precise meaning of the text is unclear, but the collocation עָרַךְ אֶל (ʿarakh ʾel, “array against”) is used elsewhere of military ({{Judges 20:30|Judg 20:30}}; 1 Chr 19:17) or verbal opposition ({{Job 32:14|Job 32:14}}).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “I will declare and I will speak, they are too numerous to recount.” The present translation assumes that the cohortatives are used in a hypothetical manner in a formally unmarked conditional sentence, “Should I try to declare [them] and speak [of them]…” (cf. NEB, NIV, NRSV). For other examples of cohortatives in the protasis (“if” clause) of a conditional sentence, see GKC 320 §108.*e*. (It should be noted, however, that *GKC* understands this particular verse in a different manner. See GKC 320 §108.*f*, where it is suggested that the cohortatives are part of an apodosis with the protasis being suppressed.) Another option is to take the cohortatives as a declaration of the psalmist’s resolve to announce the truth expressed in the next line. In this case one might translate: “I will declare and speak [the truth]: They are too numerous to recount.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “sacrifice and offering you do not desire.” The statement is exaggerated for the sake of emphasis (see {{Psalm 51:16|Ps 51:16}} as well). God is pleased with sacrifices, but his first priority is obedience and loyalty (see {{1 Samuel 15:22|1 Sam 15:22}}). Sacrifices and offerings apart from genuine allegiance are meaningless (see {{Isaiah 1:11|Isa 1:11-20}}).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “ears you hollowed out for me.” The meaning of this odd expression is debated (this is the only collocation of “hollowed out” and “ears” in the OT). It may have been an idiomatic expression referring to making a point clear to a listener. The LXX has “but a body you have prepared for me,” a reading which is followed in {{Hebrews 10:5|Heb 10:5}}.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “in the roll of the scroll it is written concerning me.” Apparently the psalmist refers to the law of God (see v. {{Psalm 40:8|8}}), which contains the commandments God desires him to obey. If this is a distinctly royal psalm, then the psalmist/king may be referring specifically to the regulations of kingship prescribed in {{Deuteronomy 17:14|Deut 17:14-20}}. See P. C. Craigie, *{{Psalm 1|Psalms 1-50}}* (WBC), 315.

*Translator's note:* Or “your will.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “your law [is] in the midst of my inner parts.” The “inner parts” are viewed here as the seat of the psalmist’s thought life and moral decision making.

*Study note:* The *great assembly* is also mentioned in {{Psalm 22:25|Pss 22:25}} and {{Psalm 35:18|35:18}}.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “I proclaim justice in the great assembly.” Though “justice” appears without a pronoun here, the Lord’s just acts are in view (see v. {{Psalm 40:10|10}}). His “justice” (צֶדֶק, tsedeq) is here the deliverance that originates in his justice; he protects and vindicates the one whose cause is just.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “Look! My lips I do not restrain.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “your justice I have not hidden in the midst of my heart.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “I have not hidden your loyal love and reliability.”

*Translator's note:* Some (cf. NIV, NRSV) translate the verb as a request (“do not withhold”), but elsewhere in the psalms the second masculine singular prefixed form, when addressed to God and preceded by לֹא (loʾ), is always indicative in mood and never has the force of a prayer (see {{Psalm 16:10|Pss 16:10}}; {{Psalm 22:2|22:2}}; {{Psalm 44:9|44:9}} {{Psalm 51:16|51:16-17}}; {{Psalm 60:10|60:10}}; {{Psalm 108:11|108:11}}; cf. NEB, NASB).

*Translator's note:* In this line the psalmist makes the transition from confidence to petition (see v. {{Psalm 40:13|13}}). Since the prefixed verbal form in the preceding line is imperfect/indicative, one could take the verb in this line as imperfect as well and translate, “your loyal love and faithfulness continually protect me” (cf. NEB). However, the כִּי (ki) at the beginning of the next verse, if causal (“because”), is best understood as introducing a motivating argument in support of a petition. For this reason v. {{Psalm 40:11|11b}} is best taken as a prayer with the prefixed form being understood as jussive (cf. NIV, NRSV). For parallels to the proposed construction (jussive followed by כִּי + perfect introducing motivating argument), see {{Psalm 25:21|Ps 25:21}}, as well as {{Psalm 10:2|Pss 10:2-3}}; {{Psalm 22:8|22:8}}.

*Translator's note:* Or “sinful deeds.” The Hebrew term used here can have a nonmoral nuance (“dangers”) or a moral one (“sinful deeds”) depending on the context. The next line (see “my sins”) seems to favor the moral sense, but the psalmist also speaks of enemies shortly after this (v. {{Psalm 40:14|14}}).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and my heart abandons me.” The “heart” is here viewed as the seat of emotional strength and courage. For a similar idea see {{Psalm 38:10|Ps 38:10}}.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “may they be embarrassed and ashamed together, the ones seeking my life to snatch it away.”

*Translator's note:* The four prefixed verbal forms in this verse (“may those…be…embarrassed and ashamed…may those…be turned back and ashamed”) are understood as jussives. The psalmist is calling judgment down on his enemies.

*Study note:* See {{Psalm 35:4|Ps 35:4}} for a similar prayer.

*Translator's note:* The prefixed verbal form is understood as a jussive in this imprecation.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “May they be humiliated according to their shame, those who say to me, ‘Aha! Aha!’”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “those who love,” which stands metonymically for its cause, the experience of being delivered by the Lord.

*Translator's note:* The three prefixed verbal forms prior to the quotation are understood as jussives. The psalmist balances out his imprecation against his enemies with a prayer of blessing upon the godly.

*Translator's note:* The prefixed verbal form is taken as a jussive, “may the Lord be magnified [in praise].” Another option is to take the verb as an imperfect, “the Lord is great” (cf. NRSV). See {{Psalm 35:27|Ps 35:27}}.

*Study note:* See {{Psalm 35:10|Pss 35:10}}; {{Psalm 37:14|37:14}}.

*Translator's note:* The prefixed verbal form may be taken as a jussive of prayer (as in the present translation; cf. NIV) or as an imperfect, “The Lord will pay attention to me” (cf. NRSV). The parallel in {{Psalm 70:5|Ps 70:5}} has, “O God, hurry to me!” For this reason some prefer to emend יַחֲשָׁב (yakhashav, “may he pay attention”) to חוּשָׁה (khushah, “hurry!”). The syntax of the Hebrew text is awkward; elsewhere when the Qal of חָשַׁב (khashav, “reckon; consider”) is collocated with the preposition ל (lamed) and a pronominal suffix there is an accompanying direct object or additional prepositional phrase/adverbial accusative (see {{Genesis 15:6|Gen 15:6}}; {{2 Samuel 19:19|2 Sam 19:19}}; {{Job 13:24|Job 13:24}}; {{Job 19:11|19:11}}; {{Job 33:10|33:10}}; {{Psalm 32:2|Pss 32:2}}; {{Psalm 41:7|41:7}}; {{Amos 6:5|Amos 6:5}}).
